builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Understanding NVIDIA Grace-Blackwell Unified Memory Through Placement-Controlled Microbenchmarks
summary: This is a measurement study, not a deployable method: it replaces reliance on a single 'Unified Memory bandwidth' figure with a placement- and history-aware cost model covering local HBM access, host-mapped access, prefetch, reuse, migration, and oversubscription eviction. Adopting its guidance costs engineering effort in explicit placement and prefetch management of managed allocations, plus benchmarking on the target platform. It fails when workloads exceed CUDA-visible memory capacity (performance drops roughly 4-5x into eviction territory) or when its GB200-specific numbers are extrapolated to the different hardware the reader actually operates.
rationale: The reader has no Grace-Blackwell hardware, so the specific measurements cannot be applied directly, but the finding that unified-memory performance depends on placement, reuse, and capacity pressure is worth tracking for future procurement or cloud-instance decisions.
technique: Placement-controlled CUDA Unified Memory characterization on Grace-Blackwell

claims.statement: This is a measurement study, not a deployable method: it replaces reliance on a single 'Unified Memory bandwidth' figure with a placement- and history-aware cost model covering local HBM access, host-mapped access, prefetch, reuse, migration, and oversubscription eviction. Adopting its guidance costs engineering effort in explicit placement and prefetch management of managed allocations, plus benchmarking on the target platform. It fails when workloads exceed CUDA-visible memory capacity (performance drops roughly 4-5x into eviction territory) or when its GB200-specific numbers are extrapolated to the different hardware the reader actually operates.

On GB200, a 1 GB triad reaches 3963 GB/s from local HBM versus 304 GB/s through host-mapped memory (about 13x); prefetched/reused managed memory exceeds 4.6 TB/s but falls to 968-1214 GB/s at 125% of CUDA-visible memory capacity.
